items.q: A 28-year-old woman bleeds heavily after delivery with an atonic uterus despite oxytocics and tamponade. The team plans uterine embolisation as fertility-sparing rescue. Which embolic agent best suits this postpartum oozing where future fertility matters and vessels should reopen?
o: Gelatin sponge as a temporary agent that recanalises
Permanent small particles to close everything
Liquid glue into both uterine arteries
items.exp:
**Answer: A - Gelatin sponge as a temporary agent that recanalises.** Sponge pledgets hold bleeding for days while the uterus recovers, then dissolve so fertility pathways reopen.
**Why the others are wrong**
- B: Permanent grains sterilise unnecessarily
- C: Glue risks permanent uterine injury
- D: Aortic coils miss uterine branches
**Key point:** Postpartum bleeding takes temporary sponge.
items.kp: Postpartum oozing suits temporary gelatin sponge.

items.q: A 45-year-old man has a 2 cm splenic artery pseudoaneurysm after pancreatitis. The sac has a narrow neck with strong inflow. The operator plans dense packing. Which coil strategy best fills this narrow-neck sac without spilling into the parent artery?
o: Framing then filling then finishing coils packed densely
One loose coil tossed into the sac
No coils with observation of large sacs
Coils placed only in the opposite limb
items.exp:
**Answer: A - Framing then filling then finishing coils packed densely.** Framing baskets outline the sac while filling and finishing loops pack it solid, holding coils off the parent artery.
**Why the others are wrong**
- B: Loose coils migrate downstream
- C: Large sacs rupture while watched
- D: Opposite limbs never fill sacs
**Key point:** Dense framing-filling-finishing packs sacs.
items.kp: Pseudoaneurysm sacs need dense staged coil packing.

items.q: A 60-year-old man has a high-flow renal fistula where standard coils keep migrating downstream on test passes. Flow measures very high through the wide feeding trunk. Which device best caps this large high-flow vessel where coils drift?
o: Vascular plug capping the wide high-flow trunk
items.exp:
**Answer: A - Vascular plug capping the wide high-flow trunk.** Self-expanding plugs grip wide walls and halt high flow where loose coils sail through like leaves.
**Why the others are wrong**
- B: Smaller coils drift further still
- C: Sponge washes out of high flow
- D: Watching lets shunts grow
**Key point:** High-flow wide trunks take vascular plugs.
r: Correct. Plugs grip wide fast flow.
items.kp: High-flow wide vessels need vascular plug capping.

items.q: A 38-year-old woman has a small facial arteriovenous nidus that coils cannot penetrate, with feeders too tiny for particles. The operator considers liquid embolic with DMSO-compatible catheters. Which penetration advantage best suits liquid embolics for this tiny nidus?
o: Liquids flow into nidus channels that coils cannot enter
Liquids stay only where injected loudly
Glue works through any standard catheter
items.exp:
**Answer: A - Liquids flow into nidus channels that coils cannot enter.** Glue and copolymer creep through microscopic channels to cast the nidus itself rather than just blocking feeders.
**Why the others are wrong**
- B: Liquids travel far beyond injections
- C: Standard catheters melt with DMSO
- D: Watched niduses bleed and grow
**Key point:** Tiny niduses need liquid penetration.
items.kp: Uncoilable niduses need liquid embolic penetration.

items.q: A 52-year-old man undergoes hepatic embolisation and develops right upper quadrant pain with fever to 38.5 degrees and nausea on day two. Blood cultures stay negative and the gallbladder looks normal. Which expected aftermath best explains pain with fever after successful tumour ischaemia?
o: Post-embolisation syndrome needing fluids with analgesia
items.exp:
**Answer: A - Post-embolisation syndrome needing fluids with analgesia.** Dying tumour releases mediators that mimic infection, settling with hydration and pain control without antibiotics.
**Why the others are wrong**
- B: Negative cultures argue against sepsis
- C: Allergy strikes within minutes
- D: Success itself causes the syndrome
**Key point:** Pain with fever after success means post-embolisation syndrome.
items.kp: Post-embolisation syndrome needs fluids with analgesia.

items.q: A 47-year-old woman with fibroids undergoes uterine embolisation and the operator picks 500-micron microspheres. The trainee asks why mid-size grains suit fibroids. Which sizing logic best explains calibrated mid-size grains for fibroid beds?
o: Mid grains lodge in perifibroid plexus without deep myometrial killing
Tiny grains always improve fibroid results
Huge grains block the aorta better
Grain size never affects tissue levels
items.exp:
**Answer: A - Mid grains lodge in perifibroid plexus without deep myometrial killing.** Mid-size spheres wedge in the fibroid rim vessels while sparing deep myometrium, balancing kill against safety.
**Why the others are wrong**
- B: Tiny grains kill healthy myometrium
- C: Huge grains block nothing useful
- D: Size sets the occlusion level
**Key point:** Fibroids take mid-size calibrated grains.
items.kp: Fibroid embolisation uses mid-size calibrated grains.

items.q: A 55-year-old man has a gastroduodenal blush with a replaced hepatic artery nearby. The operator test-injects and sees liver filling from the target branch. Which test-injection purpose best explains this pause before deploying particles?
o: Revealing dangerous shunts to normal organs before committing
items.exp:
**Answer: A - Revealing dangerous shunts to normal organs before committing.** Small test shots map where particles would travel, exposing liver or bowel filling before permanent grains fly.
**Why the others are wrong**
- B: Contrast maps rather than entertains
- C: Pre-emptive liver treatment harms
- D: Catheters drift constantly
**Key point:** Test injections expose dangerous shunts.
items.kp: Small test injections precede permanent embolics.

items.q: A 63-year-old woman has a wide-neck renal aneurysm where coils alone keep prolapsing into the parent artery. The operator inflates a balloon across the neck during coiling. Which balloon-assistance purpose best explains neck protection during sac packing?
o: Holding coils inside the sac while preserving parent flow
items.exp:
**Answer: A - Holding coils inside the sac while preserving parent flow.** The inflated balloon walls the neck shut during packing, then deflates to leave parent flow intact.
**Why the others are wrong**
- B: Balloons protect rather than pop
- C: Kidneys need their flow preserved
- D: Pressures need cuffs not balloons
**Key point:** Balloon assistance walls coils into sacs.
items.kp: Wide-neck sacs need balloon-protected coiling.

items.q: A 41-year-old man has a bleeding intercostal branch with collaterals feeding the sac from both front and back on angiography. The operator coils both sides of the rent. Which sandwich logic best explains front-and-back coils for two-ended sacs?
o: Trapping the sac from both feeding ends against collateral refilling
Filling lungs with coils as well
items.exp:
**Answer: A - Trapping the sac from both feeding ends against collateral refilling.** One-sided coils let back-door collaterals refill the sac, so both doors shut together.
**Why the others are wrong**
- B: Revenue never guides coiling
- C: Cords need protection not blockade
- D: Lungs stay coil-free
**Key point:** Two-ended sacs need sandwich trapping.
items.kp: Collateral-fed sacs need front-and-back sandwich coils.

items.q: A 50-year-old woman develops severe buttock pain with skin mottling after internal iliac embolisation with very small particles. The team recognises deep tissue ischaemia beyond the target. Which particle-size error best explains this non-target buttock injury?
o: Oversmall grains sailing past the target into gluteal branches
items.exp:
**Answer: A - Oversmall grains sailing past the target into gluteal branches.** Tiny particles ride flow beyond the intended bed into buttock branches, infarcting skin and muscle.
**Why the others are wrong**
- B: Oversize blocks safely proximal
- C: Particles persist rather than dissolve
- D: Buttocks infarct like all tissue
**Key point:** Oversmall grains cause non-target ischaemia.
items.kp: Oversmall particles cause non-target tissue injury.

items.q: A 58-year-old man has prostate artery embolisation planned and the operator studies the vesical and rectal anastomoses carefully. The trainee asks why pelvic maps matter. Which anastomosis danger best explains careful pelvic mapping before prostate grains?
o: Bladder and rectal shunts carry grains into non-target walls
items.exp:
**Answer: A - Bladder and rectal shunts carry grains into non-target walls.** Prostatic branches join bladder and rectal networks where stray grains ulcerate innocent walls.
**Why the others are wrong**
- B: Maps prevent rather than decorate
- C: Shunts carry grains readily
- D: Bladders suffer ischaemia badly
**Key point:** Pelvic anastomoses threaten bladder and rectum.
items.kp: Prostate work maps vesical and rectal anastomoses.

items.q: A 36-year-old woman has a pulmonary arteriovenous malformation with a 4 mm feeding artery and prior brain abscess. The team plans plug closure. Which paradoxical-embolism logic best explains treating lung shunts after brain abscess?
o: Lung filters lost let clots and germs reach the brain directly
items.exp:
**Answer: A - Lung filters lost let clots and germs reach the brain directly.** Pulmonary shunts bypass the lung sieve so venous germs seed brains, and closing feeders restores filtering.
**Why the others are wrong**
- B: Shunts starve rather than feed brains
- C: Abscesses never cure lung lesions
- D: Plugs close lungs rather than brains
**Key point:** Lung shunts seed brains past lost filters.
items.kp: Pulmonary shunts with brain abscess need feeder closure.

items.q: A 49-year-old man undergoes glue embolisation and the operator flushes the microcatheter with dextrose before injecting. The trainee asks why sugar water precedes glue. Which dextrose-flush purpose best explains non-ionic preparation before glue?
o: Preventing early glue polymerisation inside the catheter
Sweetening the glue taste for patients
items.exp:
**Answer: A - Preventing early glue polymerisation inside the catheter.** Ionic fluids trigger glue setting on contact, so dextrose lines the catheter to deliver liquid glue intact.
**Why the others are wrong**
- B: Taste never guides embolisation
- C: Tumours need glue rather than sugar
- D: Dissolved catheters trap glue
**Key point:** Dextrose lines catheters before glue.
items.kp: Glue embolisation needs dextrose catheter flushing.

items.q: A 66-year-old woman has glue reflux outlined along the microcatheter during nidus injection with the tip now stuck. The operator holds the catheter steady rather than yanking. Which stuck-catheter discipline best avoids vessel tearing with refluxed glue?
o: Hold steady with gentle traction only, accepting possible catheter snapping
Yank violently to free the tip
items.exp:
**Answer: A - Hold steady with gentle traction only, accepting possible catheter snapping.** Refluxed glue welds tips to walls where force tears vessels, so patience with gentle pull protects arteries.
**Why the others are wrong**
- B: Yanking tears glued vessels
- C: Deeper pushes wedge glue further
- D: Surgery stays a last resort
**Key point:** Stuck glue catheters need patience not force.
items.kp: Glue-stuck catheters need steady patience with gentle traction.

items.q: A 44-year-old man has epistaxis embolisation planned and the operator warns about blindness risk from ethmoidal collaterals. The trainee asks how eyes connect to nasal branches. Which dangerous-anastomosis logic best explains blindness after nasal embolisation?
o: Nasal branches join ophthalmic networks that feed the retina
Noses connect directly to optic nerves
items.exp:
**Answer: A - Nasal branches join ophthalmic networks that feed the retina.** Distal nasal twigs anastomose with ophthalmic branches where stray grains blind retinas permanently.
**Why the others are wrong**
- B: Nerves differ from vessels
- C: Eyes never tolerate grains
- D: Most beds lack eye connections
**Key point:** Nasal work threatens retinas via ophthalmic links.
items.kp: Epistaxis work maps ophthalmic anastomoses against blindness.

items.q: A 53-year-old woman has bronchial embolisation planned for massive haemoptysis and the operator hunts the anterior spinal artery first. The trainee asks why backs matter in chest work. Which cord-protection logic best explains spinal mapping before bronchial grains?
o: Bronchial branches share cord feeders where grains paralyse legs
Backs need treatment before chests always
items.exp:
**Answer: A - Bronchial branches share cord feeders where grains paralyse legs.** Intercostobronchial trunks give spinal branches where stray particles infarct cords, so mapping protects legs.
**Why the others are wrong**
- B: Chests wait while cords map first
- C: Cords never tolerate grains
- D: Paralysis haunts careless chest work
**Key point:** Bronchial work maps spinal feeders first.
items.kp: Bronchial embolisation maps spinal feeders against paralysis.

items.q: A 61-year-old man has a type II endoleak feeding his excluded aortic sac through lumbar collaterals. The sac grows steadily on surveillance. The team plans translumbar sac puncture with glue. Which endoleak logic best explains direct sac treatment for lumbar-fed growth?
o: Back-door collaterals refill sacs that front doors cannot reach
items.exp:
**Answer: A - Back-door collaterals refill sacs that front doors cannot reach.** Lumbar and mesenteric branches pressurise excluded sacs from behind, needing direct sac glue.
**Why the others are wrong**
- B: Watched sacs rupture while growing
- C: Growth predicts rupture directly
- D: Lumbars pressurise sacs truly
**Key point:** Lumbar endoleaks need direct sac glue.
items.kp: Growing type II endoleaks need direct sac embolisation.

items.q: A 39-year-old woman has a uterine fibroid embolisation with ovarian collaterals seen supplying the fibroid rim. The operator discusses early menopause risk. Which collateral consequence best explains ovarian failure after fibroid grains?
o: Ovarian shunts carry grains that infarct follicles
items.exp:
**Answer: A - Ovarian shunts carry grains that infarct follicles.** Utero-ovarian links stream particles into ovaries where follicles die, advancing menopause.
**Why the others are wrong**
- B: Ovaries never welcome grains
- C: Menopause haunts ovarian embolisation
- D: Fibroids never shield ovaries
**Key point:** Utero-ovarian links threaten follicles.
items.kp: Fibroid work warns of ovarian failure via collaterals.

items.q: A 57-year-old man has a splenic laceration embolised proximally with coils in the main trunk. Follow-up shows a viable spleen with small infarcts. Which proximal-sacrifice logic best explains splenic survival after main-trunk coiling?
o: Collateral networks perfuse spleens past blocked trunks
Spleens need no blood after trauma
items.exp:
**Answer: A - Collateral networks perfuse spleens past blocked trunks.** Short gastric and pancreatic branches feed spleens around coiled trunks, preserving immune tissue.
**Why the others are wrong**
- B: Spleens need blood like all organs
- C: Coils persist rather than dissolve
- D: Small infarcts spare whole organs
**Key point:** Proximal coils spare spleens via collaterals.
items.kp: Proximal splenic coils preserve spleens through collaterals.

items.q: A 48-year-old woman has varicocele-equivalent pelvic congestion with dilated ovarian veins and chronic pelvic pain. The team plans ovarian vein coil embolisation. Which reflux logic best explains coil closure of incompetent pelvic veins?
o: Blocking refluxing trunks stops pelvic venous pooling and pain
Ovarian veins never cause pelvic pain
items.exp:
**Answer: A - Blocking refluxing trunks stops pelvic venous pooling and pain.** Incompetent ovarian veins flood pelvises with stagnant blood where coils dam the reflux.
**Why the others are wrong**
- B: Coils dam rather than flood
- C: Severe pain deserves treatment
- D: Refluxing veins ache chronically
**Key point:** Pelvic congestion needs reflux trunk coils.
items.kp: Pelvic congestion suits ovarian vein coil closure.

items.q: A 65-year-old man coughs 400 mL of bright blood with a right hilar mass on CT. Bronchoscopy localises the bleeding lobe. The team plans bronchial embolisation urgently. Which urgency logic best explains immediate embolisation for massive haemoptysis?
o: Drowning in own blood kills faster than tumours
items.exp:
**Answer: A - Drowning in own blood kills faster than tumours.** Flooded airways suffocate within minutes while tumours take months, so arteries shut first.
**Why the others are wrong**
- B: Massive bleeds drown quickly
- C: Scopes localise rather than seal
- D: Waiting drowns patients
**Key point:** Massive haemoptysis embolises urgently.
items.kp: Massive haemoptysis needs urgent bronchial embolisation.

items.q: A 42-year-old man has a high-flow priapism after perineal trauma with an arteriovenous fistula on Doppler. The team plans superselective pudendal embolisation with temporary agents. Which agent-duration logic best suits traumatic high-flow priapism in a young man?
o: Temporary agents preserve erectile tissue while closing fistulae
Permanent glue in both cavernosal arteries
items.exp:
**Answer: A - Temporary agents preserve erectile tissue while closing fistulae.** Sponge closes traumatic shunts then dissolves, sparing erectile function that permanent agents would sacrifice.
**Why the others are wrong**
- B: Glue destroys erectile beds
- C: Untreated priapism fibroses organs
- D: Surgery stays a last resort
**Key point:** Traumatic priapism takes temporary agents.
items.kp: High-flow priapism suits temporary embolic closure.

items.q: A 59-year-old woman has recurrent nosebleeds from hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia with multiple mucosal spots. Cautery fails repeatedly. The team plans staged distal embolisation. Which staged logic best suits multifocal telangiectasia bleeding?
o: Staged distal closure controls spots while sparing normal mucosa
One massive proximal block cures all spots
items.exp:
**Answer: A - Staged distal closure controls spots while sparing normal mucosa.** Multifocal spots bleed in turns where staged distal grains calm each territory without necrosing noses.
**Why the others are wrong**
- B: Massive blocks necrose whole noses
- C: Genetic bleeds still need control
- D: Removal overshoots spots hugely
**Key point:** Telangiectasia bleeds take staged distal closure.
items.kp: Telangiectasia epistaxis suits staged distal embolisation.

items.q: A 51-year-old man has a bleeding duodenal ulcer that re-bleeds after two endoscopies. Angiography shows a gastroduodenal blush. The team coils the gastroduodenal trunk front and back. Which sandwich logic best explains trapping the bleeding ulcer artery both ends?
o: Dual-end trapping blocks antegrade and collateral refilling
items.exp:
**Answer: A - Dual-end trapping blocks antegrade and collateral refilling.** Rich duodenal arcades refill single-sided coils from behind, so both doors shut together.
**Why the others are wrong**
- B: Single coils refill from behind
- C: Bleeding ulcers need arterial shutoff
- D: Back doors refill routinely
**Key point:** Ulcer arteries need front-and-back trapping.
items.kp: Re-bleeding ulcer arteries need sandwich coil trapping.

items.q: A 46-year-old woman has postpartum bleeding controlled with sponge embolisation and asks about future pregnancies. The team explains recanalisation timelines. Which counselling logic best describes fertility after temporary uterine embolisation?
o: Vessels reopen within weeks while infection screening continues
items.exp:
**Answer: A - Vessels reopen within weeks while infection screening continues.** Sponge dissolves as uteri heal, and watching for infection protects future pregnancies.
**Why the others are wrong**
- B: Temporary means reopening
- C: Sponges dissolve rather than migrate
- D: Follow-up guards fertility
**Key point:** Sponge cases counsel reopening with watching.
items.kp: Temporary uterine embolisation counsels reopening with follow-up.
